newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia warlord Johnson reappointed minister.
newsitem.headline: Liberia warlord Johnson reappointed minister.

text.p: Ethnic Krahn warlord Roosevelt Johnson, whose sacking from Liberia's cabinet ignited last April's militia warfare in Monrovia, has been given a new ministerial post, state radio announced on Tuesday.
It said a meeting of the interim ruling council on Monday named General Johnson as Minister of Transport.

The appointment completes the rehabilitation of Johnson, whose dismissal from the capital precipitated seven weeks of militia battles from April 6 that devastated Monrovia and derailed a regional plan on ending six years of civil war.

The council also confirmed another Krahn, Ignatius Clay, to the post of Central Bank Governor, replacing Raleigh Seekie, a Kru. The job has alternated between the two men since January as part of a power struggle at the root of the April battles.

At least 10 nominees of Johnson's ULIMO-J militia faction were also confirmed in various senior government positions by the six-member council of state which is steering Liberia to hoped-for elections next May.
"These appointments signed by state council chairman Mrs Ruth Perry take immediate effect," said a government statement broadcast by the radio.

Johnson was the rural development minister under power-sharing arrangements in an August 1995 peace accord which originally set disarmament of Liberia's guerrilla armies and elections to be completed in a year's time.
That accord, like a dozen others before it, fell apart when the interim government sacked Johnson and then tried to arrest him on murder charges.
The ensuing battles pitting his ULIMO-J and guerrillas of rival warlords Charles Taylor and Alhaji Kromah plunged Monrovia into the most serious violence and looting since 1990.
The United States, the most influential power in the West African state founded in 1847 by freed American slaves, sent the military to evacuate foreigners, mostly non-African.
West African leaders trying to end the civil war that has killed more than 150,000 people managed to pressure warlords last month to agree a new accord setting elections for May.
The peace accord and disarmament appear to be generally on course despite scattered violations.

On Monday international relief groups agreed to resume humanitarian aid missions halted by faction violence in Liberia's southwest Cape Mount region but said they would monitor security there on a daily basis.
U.N. spokesman Kent Page said aid groups had agreed to resume convoys to civilians in the region after an assessment team visited the town of Sinje and received no form of harassment.
